title: Standard English and Formal Language
summary: What standard English is, the non-standard forms that lose marks, how to choose between formal and informal language for your audience, and how to turn informal sentences into formal ones.

blocks.text: **Standard English** is the correct, accepted form of English used in writing, school and the exam. Some forms are fine when chatting with friends, but they are **non-standard** and lose marks in writing (except inside a character's speech in a story, where they can show how the character talks).

rows: I did my homework. / I have done my homework.
Me and Adam went to the park.
Adam and I went to the park.
I didn't do anything. / I did nothing.
Everyone should bring their book if they wants.
Everyone should bring their book if they want to.
The boy what lives next door...
The boy who lives next door...

blocks.title: Me and I
blocks.text: Take the other person away and test: *Adam and I went* → *I went* ✓ (*me went* ✗). *The teacher thanked Adam and me* → *thanked me* ✓. Polite English also puts the other person **first**: *Adam and I*, not *I and Adam*.

blocks.title: Could of? Should of?
blocks.text: When we speak fast, *could've* sounds like *could of*. But the word is always **have**: *could have, should have, would have, might have, must have*.

blocks.title: Good or well?
blocks.text: **good** is an adjective (describes a noun): *a **good** singer*. **well** is an adverb (describes a verb): *She sings **well**.*

Your **audience** (who you are writing to) and **purpose** (why you are writing) decide how formal you should be. Choosing the right level is part of **Vocabulary and language** and **Creation of texts** in the writing mark scheme.

rows: letters to a head teacher, council or company / reports / news reports / balanced arguments / information texts
emails and letters to friends or family / diaries / blogs for children / speech in stories
no: *do not, I am, it is*
precise, polite words: *receive, purchase, assist, require*
used often: *It has been decided that...*
exclamation marks and questions to sound friendly
We can't wait to see the new library!
We are looking forward to visiting the new library.
Loads of kids think the playground is rubbish.
Many pupils feel that the playground needs improvement.
Can you tell me when it opens?
Could you please inform me of the opening times?
We got lots of help from the teachers.
We received a great deal of support from our teachers.
The quality of the food was disappointing.

items: get → receive / obtain
*We received your letter on Monday.*
buy → purchase
*Tickets can be purchased at the entrance.*
help → assist / support
*Volunteers will assist visitors.*
need → require
*The hall requires new chairs.*
find out → discover
*Scientists discovered that...*
lots of / loads of → many / a large number of / a great deal of
*A large number of pupils agreed.*
kids → children / pupils / young people
*Pupils of all ages enjoy the club.*
really → very / extremely
*The trip was extremely useful.*

blocks.title: Watch out for these
items: Mixing levels: starting with *Dear Sir or Madam* and then writing *Hey, that's awesome!* Keep one level all the way through.
Contractions in a formal letter or report: *don't, can't, it's* → *do not, cannot, it is*.
Text-message style: *u, gonna, wanna, lol* never belong in exam writing.
Being too stiff in an informal email to a friend: it should sound warm and chatty, not like a report.

blocks.title: Reading questions in this style
items: *Is this text formal or informal? Give two pieces of evidence.* → for example: contractions, slang, direct questions to the reader, exclamation marks (informal); passive verbs, precise vocabulary, no contractions (formal).
*Why does the writer use informal language in this blog?* → to sound friendly and speak directly to young readers.
*Find a word or phrase that shows the letter is formal.*

blocks.text: **In your writing:** before you start, look at the task and ask **Who am I writing to?** and **Why?** A letter to the head teacher needs formal, standard English. A diary entry or an email to a cousin can be informal, but it must **still** be standard English: *we were*, not *we was*.

blocks.title: مستوى اللغة
items: قبل الكتابة اسأل: لمين بكتب؟ لو لمدير أو مسؤول أو تقرير = لغة رسمية من غير اختصارات (don't / I'm).
لو لصاحبك أو يوميات = لغة غير رسمية، والاختصارات والأسئلة وعلامات التعجب مقبولة.
حتى في الكلام غير الرسمي لازم القواعد تبقى صح: we were مش we was، و could have مش could of.

items.q: Correct all the non-standard English: *Me and Hassan done the washing up but we was tired.*
items.a: *Hassan and I did the washing-up, but we were tired.*

items.q: Make formal: *The new sports hall is awesome and loads of kids use it.*
items.a: *The new sports hall is excellent, and many pupils use it every day.*

items.q: Correct: *I should of brought my umbrella.*
Correct: *Them shoes are too small for me.*
items.a: ***Those** shoes are too small for me.*

items.q: Correct: *She didn't say nothing about the trip.*
items.a: *She didn't say **anything** about the trip.* / *She said nothing about the trip.*

items.q: Correct: *The coach thanked Laila and I.*
Make formal: *Can you sort out the broken lights ASAP?*
items.a: *Could you please repair the broken lights as soon as possible?*

items.q: Formal or informal? Give one reason: *Guess what? I'm going to Siwa next week!*
items.a: **Informal**: the contraction *I'm*, the chatty question *Guess what?* and the exclamation mark.

items.q: Which is better for a letter to the council: *We need more bins* or *Our area requires more litter bins*? Why?
items.a: *Our area requires more litter bins*: it uses precise, formal vocabulary for an official reader.
